displayQuote: Those who don't know history are doomed to repeat it

meta.title: Who really said “Those who don’t know history are doomed to repeat it”? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Edmund Burke never wrote it. The line is a loose paraphrase of George Santayana’s 1905 sentence in Reason in Common Sense. Here’s the documented source.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said ‘Those who don’t know history are doomed to repeat it’?
meta.ogDescription: Not Burke. Santayana wrote ‘Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it’ in 1905 — the popular ‘doomed’ version is later drift.

answer.label: Not Edmund Burke — a paraphrase of George Santayana
answer.sourceLine: Burke did not write this. The thought — and the only documented wording behind it — is Santayana’s: “Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it,” from The Life of Reason, Volume One: Reason in Common Sense (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1905), page 284. Quote Investigator ↗ reports it has found no closely matching statement in Burke’s writings at all; the “don’t know history … doomed” phrasing is a later, newspaper-era rewrite.

source.heading: The sentence Santayana actually wrote

docMeta.dd: The Life of Reason, Volume One: Reason in Common Sense
Chapter XII, “Flux and Constancy in Human Nature” — page 284
“Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.”

source.excerpt: Progress, far from consisting in change, depends on retentiveness. When change is absolute there remains no being to improve and no direction is set for possible improvement: and when experience is not retained, as among savages, infancy is perpetual. Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it. In the first stage of life the mind is frivolous and easily distracted; it misses progress by failing in consecutiveness and persistence.
trail: 1905 — George Santayana publishes Reason in Common Sense, volume one of The Life of Reason. The sentence appears there in its only documented original form: “Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.” Full text at Project Gutenberg ↗
The scholarly edition agrees on the page. The Santayana Edition’s own quotations page cites the line as Life of Reason, Reason in Common Sense, Scribner’s, 1905, p. 284. The Santayana Edition ↗

1941 onward — the wording drifts. Quote Investigator’s chronology tracks the “doomed” form from a 1941 column in The Union-Banner of Clanton, Alabama (“Those who ignore the lesson of the past, will be doomed to repeat it”) through Walter Lippmann in 1948, Barry Goldwater in 1962, and a 1985 Waco Tribune-Herald column by Dave Campbell that credited Winston Churchill. Quote Investigator ↗

2011 — the exact Burke-credited phrasing turns up in Quote Investigator’s chronology in a Bristol Herald Courier column: “British statesman Edmund Burke said years ago that those who don’t know history are doomed to repeat it.” Quote Investigator ↗

source.excerptNote: Santayana is arguing about retentiveness — the capacity to hold on to experience — not about people who skipped history class. Wording checked against the Project Gutenberg edition of The Life of Reason.

author.name: George Santayana
author.heading: About George Santayana
author.metaLine: 1863–1952 · Spanish-American philosopher, essayist and Harvard professor
author.bio: Born in Madrid in 1863, George Santayana moved to the United States as a child and taught philosophy at Harvard from 1889 to 1912. The Life of Reason, the five-volume work he published in 1905–1906, traced reason through common sense, society, religion, art and science — and produced the one sentence almost everyone knows and almost nobody quotes correctly. He was also an essayist, poet and novelist, and died in 1952.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on, and why
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-forwarded fake Burke lines on the internet, and it is wrong twice over: Burke did not write it, and neither — in this wording — did the man who actually coined the idea.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ states it “has found no closely matching statement in the writings of Edmund Burke,” and concludes the Burke attribution is unsubstantiated. The likely seed of the confusion is a genuinely Burkean line from Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790): “People will not look forward to posterity, who never look backward to their ancestors.” That sentence is in the primary text; the famous one is not. Burke’s Works, Vol. 3 ↗

The same saying is regularly pinned on Churchill. It appears with that credit in Quote Investigator’s chronology in a 1985 Waco Tribune-Herald column by Dave Campbell, and Quote Investigator concludes the Churchill attribution is unsubstantiated. Quote Investigator ↗

Even the true originator did not phrase it this way. Santayana wrote that those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it — not “don’t know history,” and not “doomed.” The “doomed” swap appears in Quote Investigator’s chronology as early as 1941, in a column in The Union-Banner of Clanton, Alabama: “Those who ignore the lesson of the past, will be doomed to repeat it.” Quote Investigator ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The idea and the famous sentence are George Santayana’s, published in 1905, in the words “Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.” Everything after that — “doomed,” “don’t know history,” Burke, Churchill — is a century of newspaper drift. Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: The paraphrase is a smaller idea than the original
lead: Santayana was not issuing a warning about politics or war. The sentence sits in a chapter called “Flux and Constancy in Human Nature,” inside an argument that progress depends not on change but on retentiveness — the capacity to hold on to experience at all. Where experience is not retained, he writes, infancy is perpetual.

The popular rewrite quietly shrinks him. “Those who don’t know history are doomed to repeat it” is about ignorance of facts, a failure to study. Santayana’s sentence is about an inability to retain experience — a condition he ascribes to children, to barbarians, and to an old age that is “as forgetful as youth, and more incorrigible.” That is a stranger and bleaker thought than the one on the motivational poster.
detailsBody: Burke is a magnet for invented quotations, and this one is intuitively plausible on his name: he is the statesman who described society as “a partnership not only between those who are living, but between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be born.” A thinker who framed politics as an inheritance sounds like someone who would warn you about forgetting the past, and plausibility is most of what a misattribution needs.

The genuine Burke sentence in this territory is narrower and better: “People will not look forward to posterity, who never look backward to their ancestors.” It is about inheritance and obligation, not about the danger of repeating mistakes — which is precisely why it is not the quote people think they are quoting.
